1. Create a scalar scene.

2. Select the Scalar Scene 1 > Scalar 1 node and set Contour Style to Smooth Filled.

3. Select the Scalar Scene 1 > Scalar 1 > Parts node and click to the right of the Parts property. In the object selection dialog that opens, select all the nodes under the Imported Models > trn:cylinderPressureData node.

4. Select the Scalar Scene 1 > Scalar 1 > Scalar Field node.

5. Click to the right of the Function property and choose Time History:Pressure.

The scalar scene is updated to show the pressure field at the point in time specified by the Transient Display Time property of the Imported Models > trn:cylinderPressureData node. In this instance, the initial value is set to 0.0533 s.

6. Select the Imported Models > trn:cylinderPressureData node and click to the right of Transient Display Time. Use the slider bar (or its accompanying edit box) to set the value to 0.025.

The scalar scene updates to show the pressure field at 0.025 s.

Plotting the Sound Pressure Level at Different Frequencies

1. Select the Tools > Field Functions > Fft:Pressure node and set the following properties:

Determining the Group Velocity of the Disturbances

A wavenumber-frequency diagram (or fk plot) is used to determine the group velocity at which disturbances propagate along the domain.

To determine the group velocity for this simulation, first compute cross spectral densities or auto spectral densities using the data from the .trn file. Determine the range for which the data is meaningful for analysis and use this range to compute a line spatial Fourier transform. By plotting the spectra from this Fourier transform, you can compute the group velocity of the disturbances.

This section describes the steps for doing so:

1. Creating a line probe along which transient data is extracted.

2. Creating a line time history to record data from the line probe.

3. Calculating the spectral density along the line probe.

4. Calculating the line spatial Fourier transform and using it to determine the group velocity.

Acoustic Wave Modeling: Noise from a Cylinder

This tutorial demonstrates how to set up an acoustic wave simulation in Simcenter STAR-CCM+. The flow around a cylinder is used in the simulation to describe the required steps.

The Acoustic Wave model uses the theory of Acoustic Perturbation Equations (APE) to predict the noise generated by the fluid flow (which is typically incompressible flow). The Acoustic Wave solver is one-way coupled with the flow solver through this APE-based noise source term, and models the acoustic pressure field inside a specified zone of interest. Using the Acoustic Wave model in a hybrid CFD/CAA simulation produces better results (with fewer spurious effects) than a pure compressible flow simulation.

Note: The simulation in this tutorial is an example of an application where the flow past a bluff body causes the shedding of unsteady vortices. The Reynolds number in this tutorial, 6.38E4, is in the subcritical range 300 < Re <= 1.5E5. This indicates that the vortex shedding will be strong and periodic, exhibiting the familiar Karman vortex street. The onset of this phenomenon is inherently unpredictable.

The process for performing an acoustic wave simulation is as follows:

1. Perform a steady turbulent simulation to get an initial flow solution.

2. Perform an unsteady simulation to get a fully developed flow solution.

3. From the unsteady solution, compute the mean flow pressure.

4. Activate the Acoustic Wave model in the unsteady simulation.

5. Specify the noise source (the zone of interest in the flow) and the acoustic damping function to use in the acoustic wave simulation.

6. Run the acoustic wave simulation to obtain the acoustic pressure values throughout the flow region.

You can perform post-processing of the acoustic data to compare the simulation results against other data. Simcenter STAR-CCM+ provides built-in data set functions, such as Fourier Transforms, that you can use to apply signal processing to the acoustic data.

The geometry that is used in this tutorial is shown below.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10720

The geometry consists of a cylinder, 20 mm in diameter, placed at the center of a three-dimensional circular computational domain, 0.6 m in diameter. The air velocity is set to 50 m/s.

Loading the Base Simulation

A base simulation file has been prepared for this analysis. Continue by starting the simulation, loading the base simulation file, and saving it under a new file name.

To load the base simulation:

1. Start up a double precision version of Simcenter STAR-CCM+ in a manner that is appropriate to your working environment.

2. Load the base simulation file:

a) Click (Load Simulation) from the tool bar.

b) In the Load Simulation dialog, under Process Options, select Parallel on Local Host.

You are strongly advised to run acoustic wave simulations in parallel. This tutorial case has a high number of cells and uses 10 inner iterations, so can be slow to run.

c) In the Compute Processes box, set an appropriate number for the machine on which you are working.

To make the run time reasonable, 10 processors are recommended.

d) Navigate to your working directory and open cylinderBase.sim.

Maintaining the Appropriate Acoustic CFL in the Wave Equation

To maintain the accuracy of acoustic predictions, apply criteria for points per wavelength (PPW) and the Acoustic CFL. This section outlines the requirements and calculations for this case.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10722

The mesh size in the acoustic zone affects two criteria that are important for accurate acoustic predictions: the Acoustic CFL and the points per wavelength (PPW). The appropriate calculations for this tutorial are shown below.

Points Per Wavelength (PPW)

The recommended PPW for an acoustic calculation is PPW ≥ 30-40, maintained throughout the undamped zone. You can calculate the expected wavelength for this simulation from the vortex shedding frequency across the cylinder. This frequency is calculated from the Strouhal number:

St = fD v (4561)

where f is the vortex shedding frequency, D is the diameter of the cylinder, and v is the air velocity.

The settings given in this tutorial are representative for a typical industrial application, where flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number for this tutorial is Re = 6.38 ⋅104, which is within the sub-critical range

300 < Re ≤1.5 ⋅105. To obtain the correct vortex shedding frequency it would be necessary to use the Laminar model instead, according to the flow regime that the cylinder experiences.

The expected Strouhal number for this regime is St = 0.2, which corresponds to a frequency of:

f = St v D = 0.2 ⋅50/0.02 = 500 Hz

The wavelength in turn is calculated as:

λ = c/f

where c = 340 m/s is the speed of sound. As PPW = c/f /Δx, the required mesh size for PPW of 40 is:

Δx =

340 m s /5001 s 40 = 0.017 m

Acoustic CFL

For the recommended PPW of 40, aim to have Acoustic CFL ≤ 4 in the zone of interest. Acoustic CFL is defined as:

Acoustic CFL = c Δt Δx (4562)

Rearranging and inserting a time-step Δt of 2.5 ⋅10−5s gives a candidate mesh size of:

Δx = 340m s ⋅2.5 ⋅10−5s /4 = 0.002125 m

Overall Mesh Size

Taking the lower computed amount of 0.002125 m and rounding down gives a final target mesh size of 0.002 m in the acoustic zone.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10723

The meshing models and mesh reference values for this simulation have already been set up. A volumetric control has been created for mesh refinement, to capture the separation behind the cylinder, and to capture the vortex shedding.

The mesh size is 0.008 m in the coarse zone and 0.002 m in the fine zone.

To generate the volume mesh:

Obtaining the Acoustic Wave Solution

Starting from the solution of the unsteady simulation (a fully developed flow solution), activate the Acoustic Wave model, specify the noise source region, and then run the simulation to compute the acoustic pressure.

This simulation models acoustic waves that are generated by turbulent flow. You specify the noise source with a field function that defines a volume of interest within the flow region. To suppress acoustic reflections from outside the noise source volume, you specify an acoustic damping function. Physical damping is required in this case, since the mesh becomes coarse away from the region of interest.

Defining the Noise Source Region and Damping Zone

When you use the Acoustic Wave model, you specify the noise source and the acoustic damping by setting the appropriate physics conditions and physics values of the flow region.

The Acoustic Wave model requires you to define field functions for two coefficients:

• The Noise Source Weighting Coefficient, which defines the space within which noise is generated.

• The Acoustic Damping Coefficient, which Simcenter STAR-CCM+ uses to suppress acoustic reflections outside the noise source enclosure space.

In this tutorial, the NoiseZone and DampingZone field functions define these quantities, respectively. Both of these field functions use a Hanning window for the transition between the values of 0 and 1.

Summary

This tutorial demonstrated how to set up an acoustic wave simulation in Simcenter STAR-CCM+, using the flow around a cylinder.

This tutorial demonstrated how a flow-generated noise source can be identified and propagated through the zone of interest using a hybrid CFD/CAA modeling technique. In this case, noise that is generated by flow over the cylinder is captured and the noise source information is passed onto the acoustic wave solver.

This tutorial has covered the following:

• Obtaining the mean flow pressure from an unsteady flow solution.

• Selecting the Acoustic Wave model.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10740

• Specifying the noise source zone to enclose all of the important noise sources that are generated in the flow.

• Minimizing spurious acoustics: specifying the acoustic damping zone to ensure damping in the fine-tocoarse mesh transition regions away from the zone of interest.

• Setting the solver parameters and stopping criteria.

• Displaying the acoustic pressure in a scalar scene.

Acoustic Suppression Zone Modeling: Direct Noise Simulation

Unsteady aeroacoustics simulations require effective non-reflective boundary conditions to prevent spurious reflected acoustic waves from the boundaries of the computational domain interfering with the aeroacoustic results.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ provides the Acoustic Suppression Zone model, which achieves non-reflective conditions at the boundaries by damping the flow field unsteadiness within a zone of specified thickness—the acoustic suppression zone. This damping prevents the acoustic waves and vortical disturbances from reaching the boundaries and eliminates spurious back-reflected waves at the boundaries. The amount of damping is controlled by the relaxation coefficient. The relaxation coefficient ramps the damping in space from zero inside the domain up to a maximum value at the boundary. A ramping in time of the maximum Acoustic Suppression Zone relaxation coefficient is recommended to improve the robustness of the aeroacoustics simulation.

The focus of this tutorial is on demonstrating how to set up an unsteady compressible direct noise aeroacoustic simulation using Large Eddy Simulation (LES) for predicting turbulence and the Acoustic Suppression Zone model for providing non-reflective boundary conditions.

In this tutorial, you simulate the flow of a jet from a pipe expanding into the environment. The following schematic diagram shows the configuration of the pipe geometry and the boundaries:

The compressible gas, here modeled as air using the ideal gas law, enters the duct with a mass flow rate 0.15 kg/s and a total temperature of 700 K. The gas leaves the open pipe and expands into the environment, which creates unsteady flow structures and acoustic effects. The environment is bounded by a spherically shaped pressure outlet with an atmospheric pressure of 101325 Pa and a temperature of 300 K. The unsteady flow structures and sound propagate towards the pressure boundary, which requires activation of the acoustic suppression zone at the boundary to ensure that the pressure waves pass through it without reflection.

You run the tutorial simulation in two steps:

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10742

1. You perform a steady-state flow simulation with a Reynolds-Averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) turbulence model to obtain the mean field of pressure, velocity, and temperature to be used as target values for the acoustic suppression zone simulation.

2. You perform an unsteady acoustic suppression zone simulation with LES using the target values from the RANS simulation.

Prerequisites

Loading and Running the RANS Reference Simulation

Mapping the RANS Simulation Results

Selecting Physics Models for the Acoustic Suppression Zone Simulation

Specifying Acoustic Suppression Zone Boundary and Region Settings

Visualizing Pressure Fluctuations

Running the Acoustic Suppression Zone Simulation

Analyzing Results

Input File

The input file that you require for this tutorial is aeroacoustics/jetASZ_start.sim in the downloaded tutorial files.

Loading and Running the RANS Reference Simulation

For this tutorial, you are provided with an input file that contains the mesh around the pipe bounded by the spherical pressure boundary. To provide input for the acoustic suppression zone definition, you run a fully prepared steady-state RANS simulation.

Due to the large number of cells, you are advised to launch this tutorial in parallel on as many cores as feasible.

Note: Use the double precision version of Simcenter STAR-CCM+ for all aeroacoustic analyses.

To load the RANS reference simulation:

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10743

1. Launch a double precision version of Simcenter Simcenter STAR-CCM+.

2. Load an existing simulation:

a) Click (Load a File) from the tool bar.

b) In the Process Options group box, select an appropriate parallel option and set the number of Compute Process to a minimum of 4.

c) In the Load a File dialog, click Browse.

d) In the Open dialog, navigate to the aeroacoustics folder of the downloaded tutorial files and select jetASZ_start.sim.

e) Click Open.

3. Review the predefined RANS simulation:

a) To review the volume mesh, select the Scenes > Mesh node and open the scene.

The cylindrical pipe is in the center of the computational domain. A trimmed cell mesh has been created with embedded refinement and two prism layers around the jet nozzle geometry. For an acoustic suppression zone simulation, you are advised to place the surrounding outflow boundary, here the pressure outlet boundary, at a sufficient distance from the noise sources to faithfully reproduce the real acoustic behavior of the far-field, that is, far enough away from the source of the acoustic waves. To save cells, an outer ring of cells that coarsens towards the pressure outlet is extruded from an internal interface.

For aeroacoustics simulations, you bear in mind two main requirements when generating a high-quality mesh:

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10744

▪The mesh must resolve the sound-generating turbulence scales

▪The mesh must resolve the propagating acoustic waves up to the desired frequency.

Usually, to address the large disparity between the length scales of the turbulent structures and the length scales of the sound waves, the mesh that you create consists of two different areas with different mesh densities.

The cell size in the acoustic propagation area is chosen such as to resolve the acoustic waves up to an upper frequency limit, which is f = 500 Hz for this tutorial.To ensure a mesh resolution of 20 cells per wavelength (points per wavelength—PPW), you estimate the cell size as:

Δx = λ 20 =

c f 20 =

347 m/s 500 1/s 20 = 0.0347m (4563)

where λ is the wavelength and c is the speed of sound of air.

At the pressure probe, the mesh must properly resolve the acoustic waves. This requirement translates to the acoustic waves having to propagate from the source of noise, the jet nozzle, to the probes with minimal numerical dissipation. The decay in amplitude due to numerical dissipation is proportional to the propagation distance, measured in number of wavelengths. For this tutorial mesh, in the space separating the noise source from the pressure probe, the cell size is around 0.045 m, which is close to the estimated value of 0.0347 m.

You can verify if the cell size is sufficient to resolve the turbulent structures from a precursor steady RANS simulation, as this one, by using the Mesh Frequency Cutoff field function. For more information, see Visualizing the Mesh Frequency Cutoff Hz Contour.

b) To review the boundary conditions, expand the Regions > Region_1 > Boundaries node.

c) To review the physics models, expand the Continua > RANS - Steady node.

Active models:

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10745

d) To review solver settings, expand the Solvers > Segregated Flow node.

For initialization, you use a built-in initialization procedure—the Continuity Initialization. This procedure initializes the flow field by solving the continuity equation. You use it for steady-state simulations only. All other numerical settings remain at their defaults.

e) To review the stopping criterion, expand the Stopping Criteria > Maximum Steps node.

The run stops after 500 iterations.

4. Click (Run) to run the simulation.

5. To review the results of the RANS simulation, select the Scenes > Scalar - Velocity node and open the scene.

Selecting Physics Models for the Acoustic Suppression Zone Simulation

The ASZ is defined by the ASZ thickness and the maximum relaxation coefficient. Generally, the ASZ should have a thickness of 2 to 5 acoustic wavelengths, based on the lowest frequency of interest, which here is 200 Hz.

For this tutorial, the acoustic wavelength is:

λ = c f =

347m s

200 1 s = 1.735 m

The ASZ thickness can be approximated as:

Δl = 2 ⋅1.735 m = 3.47 m ≈3 m Typically, you choose the maximum relaxation coefficient value to be suitable for your ASZ simulation. For this tutorial, 200 is an appropriate value. You specify the maximum relaxation coefficient as a function of time:

Specifying Acoustic Suppression Zone Boundary and Region Settings

You perform the acoustic suppression zone simulation on the same mesh as the RANS reference simulation. Therefore, you associate the LES physics continuum with the same region that you used for the RANS reference simulation. Reflection of the acoustic disturbances emerging from the tailpipe need only be damped at the pressure boundary that confines the computational domain. You prescribe the acoustic zone target pressure, velocity, and temperature fields using the mapped mean values from the RANS reference simulation.

Prescribing the acoustic target pressure, velocity, and temperature fields at the pressure boundary allows the constant pressure value that you specify at the boundary to be treated as an average pressure. Therefore, the flow pressure at the outflow boundary can vary, thus permitting pressure disturbances to pass through the boundary and to leave the domain without being reflected.

To specify the acoustic suppression zone boundary and region settings:

1. Select the Regions > Region_1 node and set Physics Continuum to LES.

2. Select the Region_1 > Boundaries  > Pressure Outlet > Physics Conditions > Acoustic Suppression Option node and set Enable Acoustic Suppression to On.

Running the Acoustic Suppression Zone Simulation

You run the unsteady acoustic suppression zone simulation for a physical time of 0.4 s. The iterations per timestep stop when the relative change in residuals of the continuity equation is less than 2% or the maximum number of inner iterations of 15 is reached. To enhance the accuracy of the simulation, you set the temporal discretization of the implicit unsteady solver as well as those of the continuity equation and the energy equation to a second-order scheme. The time-step varies over time as a step function:

10−3 ;  if  t < 0.1 s

5 × 10−4 ;  if  0.1 ≤t < 0.15 s

10−4 ;  if  t ≥0.15 s

To speed up convergence per time-step, you increase the under-relaxation factors from their defaults.

Ohmic Heating: Domestic Fuse

This tutorial demonstrates some of the capabilities of the Ohmic Heating model available in Simcenter STAR-CCM+.

A simple domestic fuse geometry is used in the simulation to demonstrate the required steps. The geometry is shown below.

A fuse is a safety device to protect electrical equipment against unexpected high currents. Because of the Joule effect, the current going through the thin wire inside the fuse increases its temperature. If the current hits the critical current, the wire temperature exceeds its melting point, and breaks.

The fuse assembly in this tutorial is 30 mm long and is composed of metal, ceramic, and silicium. The wire inside the ceramic enclosure is 27.5 µm in diameter and has a critical current of 7 A with ±0.7% error.

A CAD model has been prepared in which various parts are imprinted correctly on adjacent parts. When this model is imported into STAR-CCM+ (as geometry parts), coincident faces are automatically detected and used to generate part contact data. The scenario being simulated is rather simple: to increase the potential difference between the two terminals of the wire, thus inducing a current increase until it reaches the critical point.

The post-processing tools in STAR-CCM+ are used to visualize the results.

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10757

Importing the Surface Mesh and Naming the Simulation

A CAD file containing the fuse assembly has been prepared for this analysis.

Begin by copying the file from the Simcenter STAR-CCM+ installation directory, starting the simulation, importing the CAD model and saving the simulation.

1. Create a directory for the tutorial called ohmicHeating.

2. In this directory, copy the files containing the problem geometry (fusePartsAssembly.x_b) and the potential levels data (potentialLevels.csv) from the electromagnetism folder of the downloaded tutorial files.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10758

3. Start up Simcenter STAR-CCM+ in a manner that is appropriate to your working environment and create a New Simulation.

4. Click (Import Surface Mesh) from the tool bar.

5. In the Open dialog, select file fusePartsAssembly.x_b.

6. Click Open to start the import.

7. In the Import Surface Options dialog that appears, do the following:

a) Select the Create New Part from the Import Mode box.

b) Make sure that Create Part Contacts from Coincident Entities option is selected.

c) Click OK to retain the default options.

STAR-CCM+ provides feedback on the import process in the Output window. In particular, note the message Created 8 new Part Contacts from 10 pairs of coincident faces. A geometry scene is created in the Graphics window.

8. Finally, save the simulation to disk under file name fuseWire.sim.

Examining the Imported Geometry

The imported CAD parts, which represent the different parts of the fuse and its holder, are contained in the Geometry > Parts manager node.

The various parts were previously imprinted on each other to provide pairs of matching faces on the surfaces that are in contact. STAR-CCM+ detects the matching faces on import, and creates part/part contact data that are used later to define interfaces between regions.

These contacting surfaces can be viewed successively as follows:

1. Right-click the Geometry > Contacts node and select Browse Part/Part Contacts.

2. In the Part/Part Contact Browser Options dialog, make sure that all the parts are selected and click OK.

The Part/Part Contact Browser dialog opens in the edit window and a scene in the Graphics window.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10759

3. Select Wire from the Source Parts menu. Use the navigation buttons under the Target Parts menu to step through the Clip+ve, Clip-ve, and Silicium parts with which the wire is in contact.

4. Click Close.

The surfaces and feature curves of geometry parts are stored as individual entities on which operations can be performed if necessary. No further operations are required in this tutorial, but it is instructive to examine the surfaces for the electric potential.

5. Open the Parts > Clip+ve > Surfaces and Parts > Clip-ve > Surfaces nodes. Multi-select the terminal+ and terminalnodes.

These surfaces are highlighted in the Graphics window.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10760

6. Use the mouse buttons to zoom in and position the part so that the view appears as shown.

7. Click (Save-Restore-Select Views) in the Vis toolbar and select Store Current View.

Increasing the Tessellation Density of the Fuse Wire

To ensure that the thin fuse wire has a well-defined surface, increase the tessellation density of the imported surface to represent the surface with a higher density of triangles.

1. Right-click the Geometry > Parts > Wire node and select Re-tessellate.

2. In the Tessellation Options dialog, set Tessellation Density to Fine.

3. Click OK.

Assigning Geometry Parts to Regions

Assign geometry parts to regions before surface or volume meshing takes place. Simcenter STAR-CCM+ allows you to create regions and boundaries that are based on the parts and their surfaces.

1. Multi-select all of the parts. Right-click the selected nodes and select Assign Parts to Regions.

2. In the Assign Parts to Regions dialog:

a) Set the Region mode to Create a Region for Each Part.

b) Set the Boundary mode to Create a Boundary for Each Part Surface.

c) The Feature Curve mode can be left at Create One Feature Curve for All Part Curves. The Create Boundary-mode Interfaces From Contacts option remains selected.

d) Click Apply and then Close.

The necessary regions and boundaries are created, along with interfaces corresponding to the part/part contact information reviewed earlier.

3. Expand the Regions and Interfaces nodes.

There are eight interfaces corresponding to the eight sets of part/part contact data.

Specifying Physics Models and Material Properties

You can now specify the physical models and the material properties for this simulation.

Three physics continua are required for this simulation:

• Copper (Ohmic Heating): For the Clip+ve, Clip-ve, and Wire regions through which electric current passes.

• Ceramic: For the Ceramic region, which is the outer casing of the central portion of the fuse.

• Silicium: Fills the annulus between the wire and the ceramic casing.

Summary

This tutorial demonstrated how to set up a simulation involving Ohmic Heating in Simcenter STAR-CCM+.

This tutorial has introduced the following STAR-CCM+ features:

• Importing a surface mesh, creating a part and naming the simulation.

• Visualizing and examining the imported geometry.

• Generating a volume mesh using a surface remesher and polyhedral mesher.

• Setting the physics models for an Ohmic heating analysis.

• Implementation of user field functions.

• Setting up report, monitors, and plots.

• Post-processing electric potential and temperature.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10778

Magnetic Vector Potential: Axial Flux Motor

This tutorial demonstrates how to use the Finite Element Magnetic Potential Vector model to solve for the magnetic flux produced by the magnets of an axial-flux motor.

An axial-flux, or “pancake”, motor is a disc-type electric motor where magnets are arrayed on a rotor around a central shaft. This type of motor is typically used in applications that require a short axial length, for example in elevators where the lifting gear is located inside the elevator shaft.

The main flux in an axial-flux motor passes through an air gap between the rotor and stator in a direction parallel to the axis of rotation. The three-dimensional magnetic flux distribution the motor produces is difficult to calculate using analytical methods.

This simulation models 1/8 of a slotless permanent-magnet brushless motor, surrounded by air. In the full geometry, magnetic poles of opposite polarity (north and south) alternate around the central shaft. In the reduced geometry, you model a single magnetic pole and use antiperiodic interface conditions to account for the change in polarity.

The windings, which would be located in the gap between the rotor and the stator, are not shown, as they are not used in the simulation.

Analysis Overview

Geometry 1/8 of the full geometry

Mesh • Linear tetrahedral elements

• Conformal interfaces

Materials and Physics Materials:

• Bounding domain: Air

• Motor Components: Steel with constant magnetic permeability (linear magnetization assumption)

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10779

Main Physics Models:

• Finite Element Magnetic Potential Vector to solve for magnetic flux density

• Permanent Magnet to model the effects of a permanent magnet

Boundary Conditions Anti-Symmetry Perfect Electric Conductor (PEC) assumption for all boundaries.

Interfaces • internal interfaces between contacting regions

• periodic interfaces with antiperiodic magnetic vector potential, to replicate the behavior of the full geometry

Discretization and Solution Method Finite Element (FE) method

Importing the Geometry

In this tutorial, you are provided with a CAD model representing 1/8 of the geometry. From this CAD model, you create geometry parts for the magnet, the magnet plate, the stator plate, and the surrounding air.

1. Launch Simcenter STAR-CCM+ and start a new simulation.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10780

2. Right-click the Geometry > 3D-CAD Models node and select New.

3. In 3D-CAD, rename the 3D-CAD Model 1 node to Axial Flux Motor.

4. Right-click the Axial Flux Motor node and select Import > CAD Model.

5. In the Open dialog, navigate to the electromagnetism folder of the downloaded tutorial files.

6. Select axialFluxMotor.x_b and click Open.

7. Close 3D-CAD.

Create geometry parts from the CAD model:

8. Expand the Geometry > 3D-CAD Models > Axial Flux Motor > Body Groups node and multi-select Air, Magnet, Magnet Plate, and Stator Plate.

9. Right-click one of the selected nodes and select New Geometry Part.

10.In the Part Creation Options dialog, click OK.

To visualize the geometry:

11.Right-click the Scenes node and select New Scene > Geometry.

12.Click (Make Scene Transparent) and position the geometry as desired.

13.Save the simulation to your working directory as axialFluxMotor.sim.

Creating Periodic Contacts

To simulate the behavior of the full geometry model, you create periodic contacts between the part surfaces of the reduced geometry.

To create a periodic contact between the side surfaces of the air domain:

2. Multi-select S1 and S2, right-click one of the selected surfaces and select Create Periodic.

To create a periodic contact between the side surfaces of the magnet:

3. Expand the Parts > Magnet > Surfaces node and multi-select S1 and S2.

4. Right-click one of the selected surfaces and select Create Periodic.

To create a periodic contact between the side surfaces of the magnet plate:

5. Expand the Parts > Magnet Plate > Surfaces node and multi-select S1 and S2.

6. Right-click one of the selected surfaces and select Create Periodic.

To create a periodic contact between the side surfaces of the stator plate:

7. Expand the Parts > Stator Plate > Surfaces node and multi-select S1 and S2.

8. Right-click one of the selected surfaces and select Create Periodic.

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10782

As the contacts have rotational periodicity, you specify the origin and direction of the axis of rotation:

◦ Air/Air > S1/S2 > Periodic Transformation

◦ Magnet Plate/Magnet Plate > S1/S2 > Periodic Transformation

◦ Magnet/Magnet > S1/S2 > Periodic Transformation

◦ Stator Plate/Stator Plate > S1/S2 > Periodic Transformation

Preparing the Regions and Generating the Mesh

Assign the geometry parts to regions, creating the required boundaries and interfaces, and generate a mesh of tetrahedral elements. Tetrahedral elements are suitable for finite element solvers.

Create a region for each motor component and the air domain:

1. Expand the Geometry > Parts node and multi-select all parts.

2. Right-click one of the selected parts and select Assign Parts to Regions.

3. In the Assign Parts to Regions dialog, select the following options:

Create a Region for Each Part Create a Boundary for Each Part Surface

The default interface option is appropriate.

4. Click Apply then Close.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ adds the required regions and boundaries and creates internal interfaces between the regions. The interfaces that originate from periodic contacts have periodic topology.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Running the Simulation

Freeze the flow solver and run the simulation to solve for the magnetic flux.

As this is a linear problem, the FE Sparse Direct Solver computes the solution in one iteration. For linear problems, it is good practice to make sure that the residuals drop at least 6 orders of magnitude within the second iteration.

1. Select the Stopping Criteria > Maximum Steps node and set Maximum Steps to 2.

In this simulation, the only variable of interest is the magnetic flux. Therefore, you can freeze the flow solver to speed up the computation:

2. Select the Solvers > Segregated Flow node and activate Freeze Flow.

Magnetohydrodynamics: Stirring Induced by Excitation Coils

In this tutorial, you simulate the electromagnetic stirring of molten metal induced by excitation coils.

The molten metal is contained within a cylindrical ladle that is surrounded by excitation coils. The electric current flowing through the coils induces a force (the Lorentz force) that acts on the electrically conducting fluid, stirring the metal. The ladle and coils are contained within a vacuum chamber.

As the problem has cylindrical symmetry, the 3D geometry is converted to a 2D mesh and the problem is solved in the axisymmetric space.

As the electric current in the coils is sinusoidal, it is convenient to perform the electromagnetic analysis using the Harmonic Balance FV Transverse Magnetic Potential model.

Analysis Overview

Geometry and Mesh 2D Axisymmetric

Physics and Assumptions Excitation Coils:

• 5 coils modeled as a single region, in contact with the environment

• sinusoidal electric current, with peak current of 200 A, and frequency of 50 Hz

• eddy currents are neglected

Liquid Metal:

• electrically conducting fluid in contact with the environment

• laminar regime

• eddy currents are included

Environment:

• vacuum

• eddy currents are neglected

• outer boundary is assumed to be a perfect electric conductor (PEC)

Airgap Remeshing: Electronic Speedometer

Electric machine simulations require a conformal mesh at the interfaces between different components. Airgap remeshing is a meshing technique that allows you to generate and maintain conformal meshes between regions that are in relative motion.

In this simulation, you model a simple device that consists of a magnet and a pair of coils. The magnet has prescribed rotation motion, whereas the coils are fixed. As the motion of the magnet induces a voltage in the excitation coils, the coils act as a sensor to the motion of the magnet and can be used to measure the rate at which the magnet rotates. Electronic speedometers are based on this simple model.

The geometry for this tutorial consists of several parts that represent the magnet, the coils, and the surrounding environment (air). To keep the mesh conformal at the sliding interface, the air domain is divided into multiple portions of which only two are remeshed during each time-step. These two portions are thin and each represents one side of the interface between the moving zones. The other parts of the air domain do not require remeshing. As the problem is symmetric, you only model a 45 degree sector of the geometry and use periodic interfaces.

This tutorial demonstrates a general meshing strategy for electric machine simulations. Complex parts are meshed using a tetrahedral volume mesher. The surface mesh from this complex portion is then extruded into portions of the mesh that have regular shapes. As the geometry in the tutorial is simple, the approach is not strictly necessary here.

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10804

Creating Periodic Contacts

In this simulation, you only model a 45 degree sector of the full geometry. To simulate the behavior of the full geometry, you create periodic contacts between the side surfaces of the sector geometry. For airgap remeshing, you also require periodic contacts between the rotating and the fixed airgap parts. These periodic contacts for the airgap are used in defining a repeating interface.

The starting simulation already contains periodic contacts between the side surfaces of the main air domain. To create a periodic contact between the side surfaces of the fixed airgap parts:

1. Expand the Geometry > Parts > Airgap_Fixed > Surfaces node.

2. Multi-select Left and Right, right-click one of the selected surfaces and select Create Periodic.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10810

3. Expand the Geometry > Parts > Airgap_Fixed_Extrusion > Inherited Parts > Airgap_Fixed node.

4. Multi-select Left and Right, right-click one of the selected surfaces and select Create Periodic.

5. Using the same procedure, create a periodic contact between the Left and Right surfaces of the Airgap_Rotating part.

6. Finally, create a periodic contact between the Left and Right surfaces of the Airgap_Rotating_Extrusion > Inherited Parts > Airgap_Rotating part.

The airgap remeshing process requires a repeating interface between the rotating airgap region and the fixed airgap region. To create this interface, you require periodic contacts between the rotating and fixed airgap parts.

Before you create the periodic contacts, delete any existing in-place contact between these parts:

Creating the Interfaces

Setting up a simulation with airgap remeshing requires that you manually define interfaces. For airgap remeshing, you require a repeating interface between the airgap regions.

For this simulation, you create three types of interfaces:

• in-place interfaces, including internal interfaces between parts of the same region, and contact interfaces between contacting regions

• periodic interfaces between the side surfaces of the air regions

• a repeating interface where remeshing occurs, that is, between the airgap fixed region and the airgap rotating region

At every time-step, Simcenter STAR-CCM+ remeshes the airgap regions, whereas the rest of the mesh remains fixed. The entire mesh remains conformal throughout the operation.

The Airgap Remeshing model requires you to specify the mesh operation that is executed at every time-step. When the meshing pipeline for the airgap includes multiple dependent operations, you only specify the last operation that is executed, which, in this simulation, is the volume extruder. At every time-step, Simcenter STAR-CCM+ automatically finds all dependencies and execute the required operations in order:

3. Select the Continua > Void > Models > Airgap Remeshing node and set Mesh Operations to Airgap Volume Extruder.

The following tutorial demonstrates chemical reactions induced by an electrical current.

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10827

Electroplating

Electroplating is a technique that is commonly used in industry to deposit a metal coating on parts. The part that requires coating sits within an electrolytic solution that contains metal ions. A current is then induced through the electrolyte, between the part acting as the cathode, and an anode that is made of the same metal as the metal ions. In this tutorial, you simulate electroplating of a plastic grille part, which is pre-coated with copper and nickel, using chromium ions.

In this tutorial, a voltage difference is applied between a chromium anode and a cathode that is formed from a plastic grille that already has a coating of copper and nickel. The voltage difference drives positively charged chromium ions (Cr3+) through the electrolyte from the anode to the cathode. When the Cr3+ ions reach the surface of the cathode, they gain electrons from the cathode and form chromium atoms. Since the metal chromium atoms are insoluble, they remain on the surface of the cathode to form a thin plate layer. As electrons move through the circuit from the anode to the cathode, metal chromium atoms at the anode lose electrons and become chromium ions in solution.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10828

In this tutorial, the plastic grille part is held in the electrolyte solution by a metal rack which conducts electrons from the circuit to the grille part. The plastic grille is already coated with thin layers of copper and three types of nickel. The metal rack is coated in paint to prevent it becoming plated, although it is exposed near each point of contact with the grille. The conductivity of the metal rack is much greater than the conductivity of the electrolyte or the previously plated material. Therefore, ohmic losses are negligible and the electric potential in the rack is considered to be constant. A constant electric potential boundary condition is defined at the contact points between the rack and the grille.

Since the electrolyte solution is water-based, and hydrogen ions are reduced more easily than chromium ions, passing an electric current through the solution also creates hydrogen gas at the cathode surface.

2H+ + 2e− H2 (4564)

This unwanted side reaction consumes part of the electric current. In this tutorial, the detailed reaction mechanism is not modeled. Instead, the aggregate polarization curve is imported from a table [903], and a Faraday efficiency factor accounts for the fraction of current that is associated with the metal deposition reaction.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ ensures that current is conserved in the bulk electrolyte and metal shell using the following current conservation equations:

▿⋅J = 0 (4565)

J = −σ ▿ϕ (4566)

where:

• J ≡ current density vector

• σ ≡ electrical conductivity

• ϕ ≡ electric potential

At the interface between fluid and solid domains, where electrochemical reactions occur, Simcenter STAR-CCM+ incorporates a direct linearization of the following term:

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10829

J ⋅n = j η (4567)

η = ϕsolid −ϕfluid −Ueq (4568)

Ueq ≡ equilibrium potential at zero current

j η  is a non-linear function which the Butler-Volmer, Tafel, or Tabular Polarization Curve describe.

The current density at the interface represents the total current for all electrochemical reactions at the surface. Side reactions, such as the evolution of hydrogen gas, result in a decrease in efficiency. Therefore, the efficiency of the surface mechanism that is used represents the amount of current which goes towards the plating reaction. This mechanism is based on the current densities that are calculated at the cathode, according to Song and Chin [903], at electric potentials that are relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE).

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10830

Depending on the reason for electroplating parts, the thickness of the metal coating can become significant. If the coating is intended to protect the part from corrosion, then a thicker coating is required than if the coating is for decorative purposes. In this tutorial, the thickness of the pre-coated layer is approximated as the constant thickness of the shell region that represents the coating. To model a more accurate representation, you can run a transient simulation which accounts for the changing thickness at each time-step.

The thickness of the chromium plating is calculated using the following equation:

d = θ M zFρ jΔ t (4569)

where:

• d is the plating thickness [m]

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10831

• M is the molecular mass of the metal plating, which in this case is 51.99 for chromium [kg/kmol]

• z is the charge of metal ion, which in this case is 3.

• F is the Faraday constant, which is 96,485,336.5 [s A/kmol].

• ρ is the plated metal mass density, which in this case is 7.19 × 103 [kg/m³]

• Δ t is the plating time, which in this case is 300 [s]

• j is the current density (Boundary Specific Electric Current) which is returned from the simulation by a field function [A / m²]

• θ is the plating efficiency. The Song_Cr3+Polarization table contains lists of plating efficiencies at various current densities. This data is interpolated to return plating efficiencies at the local values of current density (Boundary Specific Electric Current).

When running the tutorial, the thickness of the chromium coating and the electric potential of the cathode (grille) are monitored using scalar scenes. If the current at the cathode drops, the rate of electrodeposition of chromium also drops. Therefore, you also plot the electric current at the anode and the cathode.

Running the Simulation and Reviewing the Results

After running the simulation, you can view the results using the scalar scenes and plots that are set up.

The default Solver settings are suitable for this simulation.

1. Select the Stopping Criteria > Maximum Steps node and set Maximum Steps to 50.

2. Click (Run).

3. When the simulation is complete, open the Grille Electric Potential scene.

The Graphics window displays the electric potential values on the grille part.

4. Open the Cr3+ Plating Thickness scene.

The Graphics window displays the thickness of the chromium plating on the grille part.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10837

5. To check that the current is conserved between the anode and the cathode, open the Plots > Reports Plot node.

The Graphics window displays the current at the anode and the cathode.

Ohmic losses and variations in electric potential within the pre-plated shell can cause the plating of the chromium to become more localized near the points of contact between the rack and grille. Further studies

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10838

with this simulation could include observations of how the thickness of the copper and nickel shell affects the plating process. A thinner shell results in wider variations in electric potential values throughout the shell, which affects the amount of chromium that forms on the surface of the shell. For instability troubleshooting, modify the electric potential initial conditions and/or decrease the electric potential under-relaxation factor in the solver settings.

Solid Oxide Fuel Cell

Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs) harness the chemical energy that is released by electrochemical reactions and convert it to electrical energy. SOFCs typically consume hydrogen and oxygen and only produce water as a waste product.

SOFCs are electrochemical cells (or stacks of cells) which are composed of electrodes (an anode and a cathode), a solid oxide electrolyte, and current collectors.

This tutorial demonstrates the workflow for setting up and simulating a single planar button solid oxide fuel cell. The mole fraction of oxygen is visualized in relation to the reaction flux. It is important to check that the transport of oxygen through the cathode is sufficient enough to avoid oxygen starvation—which would limit the reaction rate and damage the fuel cell components. Setting up a case in this way with a single cell is useful to first determine the optimal set-up, transport mechanism, and reaction mechanism before scaling-up to simulate multiple cells in a stack.

The following diagram shows the different components of the planar button SOFC.

The planar button SOFC is placed inside a cylindrical casing. The complete geometry consists of an external casing which is intersected by the solid oxide electrolyte membrane and the anode and cathode current collectors. Within the volume of the external casing, there are internal aluminium tubes. Products of the reactions leave the SOFC from the space between the external casing and the tubes.

Components Key Features

Solid Oxide Electrolyte Membrane • Solid Shell Region

• Thickness 0.06mm

• Uses Solid Ion Model (identifies ions in the solid which participate in electrochemical reactions)

• Uses Electrochemical Reactions Model (solid ions participate in reactions)

Anode and Cathode Porous Regions (reactive species are not modeled in here—so no Electrochemical Reactions model required)

Anode and Cathode Current Collectors Solid Regions which can conduct an electric current

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10840

Components Key Features

Air and Fuel • Fluid Regions

• Multi-Component Gas Mixtures

• Use Electrochemical Reactions Model (air and fuel species participate in reactions)

Tubes Solid Regions

A gas phase fuel mixture (97% hydrogen and 3% water vapour) enters through the centre of the inner aluminum tube that is coincident with the anodic side of the button cell. A gas phase air mixture (21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen) enters through the centre of the inner aluminum tube that is coincident with the cathodic side of the button cell. The hydrogen in the fuel stream diffuses through the porous anode and reacts at the interface to the solid oxide electrolyte membrane. This interface represents the catalyst layers which include the triple phase boundaries, and will therefore be referred to as the TPB.

In Simcenter STAR-CCM+, the direction of the electrochemical reaction current is positive in the direction of the solid to the fluid. In many electrochemical set-ups, this direction of reaction current is suitable as the solid is the electrode and the fluid is the electrolyte. However, in SOFCs, the solid oxide membrane is the electrolyte and the fluid is within the porous electrode. The Solid Ion model in Simcenter STAR-CCM+ is in reduction

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10841

current convention, leading to negative SOFC anode current density (electrons move from the anode to the cathode). Therefore, the anodic reaction—which is an oxidation reaction:

H2 + O2 − H2O + 2e− (4570)

is given in the reduction form:

H2O + 2e− H2 + O2 − (4571)

Prior to participating in the reaction at the anode, the oxide ions are transported across the solid oxide membrane. These oxide ions are created by the reaction that occurs at the surface between the cathode and the solid oxide electrolyte membrane:

1 2O2 + 2e− O2 − (4572)

Loading an Existing Simulation

For this tutorial, you use an existing simulation file that contains pre-prepared geometry, mesh, regions, and interfaces. A selection of field functions are also supplied as a java macro file.

Defining Electrochemical Reaction Properties Using Field Functions

You use custom field functions to define enthalpies, thermodynamic polynomial data, the equilibrium potential, and the equilibrium potential temperature derivative for all reactions within the fluid domains of the fuel cell.

For convenience, these field functions can be set up by running a macro.

To create the user field functions:

1. Select File > Macro > Play Macro.

2. In the Open dialog, select sofc_setupFieldFunctions.java.

3. To run the macro, click Open.

4. Save the simulation.

For detailed information about these field functions, see Appendix: User Field Function and Parameters Properties.

Plotting the Conservation of Current, Energy, and Mass

In this part of the tutorial, you set up reports and generate monitors and plots. These plots check the balance of current, energy, and mass, respectively, throughout the solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC).

You display the results on the following plots:

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10854

• Current Conservation

The current conservation plot compares the electric current on the anode and cathode current collector boundaries to the current on the anode and cathode triple phase boundaries (TPB).

• Energy Conservation

The energy that is generated from the SOFC is not entirely converted to external electrical power. Some energy is lost as heat at the outlet. The energy conservation plot balances the external power that is generated Eqn. (4577) with the flow boundary enthalpy losses Eqn. (4576).

The non-isothermal energy conservation equation is:

Σ i, IN Hi TIN Yim˙ − Σ i, OUT Hi TOUT Yim˙ + Σ i, Reaction Hi TR m˙ i + QO + QE = 0 (4574)

where TIN and TOUT are the temperatures at the inlet and outlet respectively. m˙  is the mass flux and Yi is

the mass fraction of species i. The enthalpy of formation, Hi of species i, that is associated with the mass

that is consumed by the reaction, is converted to internal electrochemical heat (QE), internal Ohmic heat

(QO), and external electric power (P):

Σ i, Reaction Hi TR m˙ i + QO + QE + P = 0 (4575)

combining Eqn. (4574) and Eqn. (4575), gives:

P = Σ i, IN Hi TIN Yim˙ − Σ i, OUT Hi TOUT Yim˙ (4576)

The electrical power that is available to the external circuit is calculated by the anode-cathode potential difference, U, and the total current that is available to the external circuit, I:

P = IU (4577)

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ calculates the ohmic heating by accounting for electric potential losses throughout every electrically or ionically conductive substrate:

QO =∭σ ∇ϕ 2dV (4578)

where σ is the electrical conductivity and ∇ϕ is the electric potential gradient.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ calculates the electrochemical heat that is released from a reaction, i, using:

QE =∬i η + T∂Eeq ox

∂T P

(4579)

where η is the overpotential and

∂Eeq ox

∂T P is the equilibrium potential temperature derivative.

• Mass Conservation

The mass conservation plot compares the mass that is gained by the gas streams to the mass that is produced by electrochemical reactions at the TPB.

Running the Simulation

For highly diffusive problems like this, increasing the under-relaxation factors of the solvers helps accelerate convergence. With electromagnetic forces being strong forces in their nature, it is important to have well converged simulation results for the electrodynamic potential before converging the other physical quantities like the flow velocities, or species concentrations. In Simcenter STAR-CCM+, convergence can be achieved by using under-relaxation factor ramps for the latter models.

Specify solver settings and stopping criteria, and run the simulation:

1. Edit the Solvers node and set the following properties:

Note that velocity and pressure solvers must generally operate with consistent under-relaxation parameters, see section Segregated Flow Guidelines. The above settings avoid specialized ramps for the pressure solver by ramping the velocity solver discontinously from 0 to the final (default) value, where a zero under-relaxation implies a frozen flow solver.

2. Select the Stopping Criteria > Maximum Steps node and set Maximum Steps to 500.

3. Click (Run).

When the simulation is complete, review the scenes and plots.

2. Open the Reaction Flux O2 scene.

In the area of the cathode with a low concentration of oxygen, the reaction rate with respect to oxygen is decreased. The decreased reaction rate shows that the rate is limited by the concentration of oxygen, which is limited by the diffusion rate of oxygen through the porous cathode.

3. Open the Current Conservation, Energy Conservation, and Mass Conservation plots.

Summary

This tutorial demonstrated electrochemistry for a solid oxide fuel cell.

The features that were demonstrated include:

• Defining the SOFC specific user field functions for electrochemical reaction properties.

• Selecting electrochemical surface reaction models.

• Defining and assigning electrochemical surface reactions.

• Specifying region and boundary conditions.

• Preparing reports and monitor plots.

• Examining the results in the plots.

Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell

Proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy by spatially separating electrochemical reactions. Ions are transported across the polymer electrolyte membrane, and electrons are transported through an external circuit—from which electrical power is harnessed.

PEM fuel cells are useful for powering low temperature applications in portable devices, or in the transport industry.

Hydrogen is supplied at the anode where it diffuses through a gas diffusion layer (GDL). When hydrogen reaches the PEM—where a platinum catalyst is present, hydrogen splits into hydrogen ions (protons) and electrons.

Reaction at the anode:

H2 g 2H+ + 2e− (4606)

The electrons travel from the anode to the cathode through an external circuit, and the hydrogen ions pass through the PEM to the cathode. Oxygen is supplied at the cathode, where it also diffuses through a GDL and in the presence of electrons, forms oxygen ions. The hydrogen ions and oxygen ions react at the boundary between the cathode GDL and the PEM, to form water and heat.

Reactions at the cathode:

1 2O2 g + 2H+ m + 2e−s H2O g (4607)

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10873

1 2O2 g + 2H+ m + 2e−s H2O l (4608)

Anodic and cathodic reactions complement each other by consuming and producing ions and electrons in a conservative manner. The electrons travel through the external circuit from anode to cathode, up the potential gradient, due to their negative charge. Fuel cells typically operate at a positive voltage:

U = ϕcatℎode −ϕanode (4609)

Electric power is generated by the flow of electrons from the anode through the external circuit to the cathode.

During operation of a PEM fuel cell, water exists in three phases—water vapor, liquid water, and dissolved (ionomer) water requiring a multiphase treatment to describe the water transport characteristics. Water transport through the membrane, catalyst layer, and the porous gas diffusion layer has a significant impact on the cell performance.

For better cell performance, the gaseous reactants are usually humidified before entering the gas flow channel. The water vapor then diffuses through the gas diffusion layer (GDL). In the membrane, water can exist in liquid phase, in gaseous phase, and in a dissolved phase. At the anode catalyst layer, water vapor is absorbed into the membrane. The water molecules move with the protons towards the cathode catalyst by means of electro-osmotic drag. At the cathode catalyst, water is generated at the solid catalyst surface.

Sorption reactions at the anode and the cathode:

H2O g H2O m (4610)

H2O l H2O m (4611)

H2O m  denotes polar charged water molecules that are dissolved in the solid membrane.

The purpose of this tutorial is to demonstrate how to set up and run a PEM fuel cell (PEMFC) simulation in Simcenter STAR-CCM+. The following image shows the geometry that is used in this tutorial:

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10874

A water saturated fuel gas mixture of 0.8/0.2 moles hydrogen to water enter the anode channel at an inflow velocity of 1 m/s and at a temperature of 60 °C. In counter-flow, a humidified air mixture of 0.168 moles O2, 0.132 moles of N2, and 0.2 moles of H2O enters the cathode channel at a velocity of also 1 m/s. The fuel and air streams are modeled using the Eulerian Multiphase Mixture (MMP) model to account for the liquid water phase in the fuel and air streams.

The anode and cathode gas diffusion layers are specified as porous regions. Darcy’s law is employed to account for the viscous porous slip velocity between the Eulerian multiphase mixture phases. Deviation from Darcy’s law can be related to capillary forces, which are proportional to saturation curve correlations using the Leverett function [917].

The anode and cathode current collectors are both modeled as solids with Segregated Energy and Electrodynamic Potential models. The boundary conditions for the outer current collector surfaces are set to fixed potentials of 0.0 V and 0.2 V.

The proton exchange membrane (PEM) is modeled as a solid material using the Solid Ion model to define the H2O(m) electrochemical species in the sorption reaction Eqn. (4610) and Eqn. (4611). In combination with the species transport option of the Electric Potential model, migration of dissolved water through the membrane due to electro-osmotic drag is mimicked.

The porous catalyst layer is assumed to be infinitely thin and is not resolved geometrically. The anodic and cathodic reactions Eqn. (4607) and Eqn. (4608) are represented by 2D electrochemical surface reactions on the interface between the proton exchange membrane and the gas diffusion layers. The Electrochemical Reactions model is used to model the potential change across the reacting interface. The production or consumption of multi-component gas species by electrochemical reaction is calculated automatically.

Defining PEMFC Field Functions and Parameters

You use custom field functions and global parameters to define various modeling parameters of the PEM fuel cell. For convenience, you set up these field functions and parameter by running a macro.

To define the PEMFC field functions and parameters:

1. Click (Play Macro).

2. In the Open dialog, select pemfcFieldFunctions.java and click Open.

3. Save the simulation.

For detailed information about these field functions, see PEMFC Field Functions and Parameters.

Creating the Physics Continua

The components of the PEMFC (proton exchange membrane fuel cell) can be divided into three different groups with similar properties.

Since the proton exchange membrane (PEM) is unique from the other components, its physics is defined within one solid continuum, called MEM. The anode and cathode channels, and the anode and cathode gas diffusion layers, contain fluids—the physics for these components is defined within the MMP continuum. Finally, the physics for the solid anode and cathode current collectors is defined within the Solid continuum.

The reactions that occur at the interface between the proton exchange membrane and the gas diffusion layers are defined within the MMP continuum. However, the physics for the solid MEM continuum must be set up before defining any reactions.

To create the physics continua:

1. Expand the Continua node and create two further physics continua.

2. Rename the continua as follows:

Physics Continuum Name

Physics 1 MEM

Physics 2 MMP

Physics 3 Solid

Contents:

Setting up the Physics for the Proton Exchange Membrane

Setting up the Physics for the Gases and Gas Diffusion Layers

Setting up the Physics for the Anode and Cathode Current Collectors

Setting up the Physics for the Proton Exchange Membrane

You define the physics for the MEM continuum which represents the proton exchange membrane.

The anode and the cathode are separated by an ionomer membrane—like Nafion. Nafion consists of long polymer molecules with functional side-chain cations. The fixed cations are responsible for absorbing protons and water for transport across the membrane. As a result of electroneutrality, it is assumed that proton concentration does not vary through the membrane—therefore, the only driving force across the membrane is from the electric field. Given this assumption, proton flux is represented by the current density vector j in the Simcenter STAR-CCM+ Electrodynamic Potential model.

∇j = 0 ; j = −σMEM cw, T ∇ϕ (4612)

where current density is driven by a gradient in electric potential ϕ. The electrical conductivity σMEM is highly

dependent on the water concentration in the membrane cw, and temperature T. Water concentration transport

through the membrane is controlled by diffusivity Dw and electro-osmotic drag.

You select the Solid Ion model which you set to use one-way coupling including drift flux / migrative contributions from the Electric Potential model to the Solid Ion model. Also, it is important that charge

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10877

You use the Solid Ion model to define the electrochemical species that migrate through the membrane. When simulating sorption reactions and a charge is specified for the Solid Ion species, it is important to select a suitable transport option which specifies that charge conservation is not enforced.

2. Select the MEM > Models > Solid Ion node and set Transport to Electric Potential > Species.

3. Define the electrochemical species.

a) Right-click the Solid Ion > Electrochemical Species Components node and select Select Mixture Components.

b) In the Select Mixture Components dialog, expand the Material Databases node and select H+ (Hydride).

c) Click Apply, then click Apply once more, then click Close.

d) Rename the H+2 node to H2O+.

Water molecules are defined with a positive charge since the slight positive polar charge near the hydrogen atoms cause the water molecules to move through the membrane in the same direction as the positive hydrogen ions.

4. Select the Electrochemical Species Components > H+ node and set Minimum Allowable Concentration to 1.0 kmol/m^3.

The proton exchange membrane in this tutorial is modeled to replicate the properties of Nafion which allows movement of positive ions through its pores. A one molar initial concentration, zero mobility, and near infinite diffusion coefficient are used for H+ to ensure zero concentration gradients and no effect on electrochemical reactions. The intention is to highlight the lack of H+ concentration modeling and mimic hydrogen being associated with fixed cation sites within Nafion.

Setting up the Physics for the Gases and Gas Diffusion Layers

You define the physics for the MMP continuum which represents the fluid streams in the channels and the gas diffusion layers (GDL).

To account for the two-phase nature of the flow of the fuel and air streams due to the presence of liquid water, you use the Eulerian Multiphase Mixture model.

To set up the physics for the gases and the gas diffusion layers:

1. For the MMP continuum, select the following models in order:

Node Property Setting

Mixture Multiphase (MMP) Compressibility Enhancement Activated

Flow Boundary Diffusion Deactivated

Segregated Flow Flow Boundary Diffusion Deactivated

Segregated Multiphase Temperature Flow Boundary Diffusion Deactivated

Activating Compressibility Enhancement stabilizes the multiphase mixture model for highly compressible flow. Deactivating Flow Boundary Diffusion allows for the mass/mole fraction boundary conditions not to be influenced by diffusion—useful for highly diffusive flows, or when the flow boundaries are near reaction sites.

3. Save the simulation.

Setting up the Physics for the Anode and Cathode Current Collectors

You define the physics for the Solid continuum which represents the anode and cathode current collectors.

The anode and cathode current collectors are both modeled as solid with segregated energy and electrodynamic potential models. The boundary conditions for the outer current collector surfaces are set to fixed potentials.

Creating the Gas and Liquid Phases

You specify the gas and liquid phases using the Eulerian Multiphase Mixture model to represent a watersaturated fuel gas mixture, and a humidified air mixture. You define the gas phase mixtures of fuel and air as multicomponent segregated species assuming ideal gas mixtures and using NASA polynomial thermodynamic data.

To create the gas and liquid phases:

1. Right-click the MMP > Models > Multiphase > Eulerian Phases node and select New.

2. Repeat step 1 and create a second phase.

The porous viscous resistance of a phase changes depending on the volume fraction of that phase in a flow.

Although this tutorial aims to provide as realistic a set-up as possible, to assist useabilty, the intrinsic

permeability value that is used to calculate the porous viscous resistance is set to 10−9m2—in reality,

Specifying phase interaction area exponents allows you to modulate the electrochemical reaction rates (including sorption rates) depending on the volume fraction of the involved reactants. Clogging occurs due to liquid formation as a bi-product of electrochemical reaction. The clogging factor CF depends on the unresolved geometry of the mixture-multiphase (MMP) state as well as the phase interaction area exponents κp. CF

modifies the boundary species electrochemical reaction flux as given by:

CF = Π p

αp

κp (4614)

Where αp is the volume fraction of phase p.

Setting Up Reactions at the PEM/GDL Interfaces

An infinitely thin platinum catalyst layer is assumed to be present at the interfaces between the PEM and the GDLs. In this tutorial, the electrochemical reactions model is used to define these reactions at the interfaces.

To define the reactions that occur at the interface between the PEM and the anode GDL:

1. Select the Interfaces > AnodeGDL/Membrane > Physics Conditions > Electrochemistry Mechanism Option node and set Mechanism to Anodic.

Define the reactions that occur at the interface between the PEM and the cathode GDL.

2. Select the Interfaces > CathodeGDL/Membrane > Physics Conditions > Electrochemistry Mechanism Option node and set Mechanism to Cathodic.

3. Save the simulation.

Battery Simulation Module: Cell Thermal Analysis

This tutorial introduces the battery modeling capabilities of Simcenter STAR-CCM+. It simulates the battery heat generation that occurs during the first 90 seconds of a discharge cycle.

The tutorial takes you through the steps that are required to run a battery analysis in Simcenter STAR-CCM+ using files that are created in Battery Design Studio® (BDS).

Additional licenses are required to use the battery modeling capabilities:

• For battery modeling, Simcenter STAR-CCM+ requires a batterysim license in addition to the other license features.

• BDS, which is supplied for use with the Simcenter STAR-CCM+ battery modeling capability, requires a batterydesignstudio license.

The tutorial is divided into three parts:

1. Preparing files in BDS

2. Running a Simcenter STAR-CCM+ simulation with a Single Cell

3. Running a Simcenter STAR-CCM+ simulation with 3 Cells in Series

The battery heat generation that occurs during the first 90 seconds of a discharge cycle is simulated. A simple scenario with a single cell battery is run first. The simulation is then rerun after modifying the battery, adding two more cells in series.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10911

Both simulations use a voltage plot to monitor the battery discharge during the cycle. A scalar scene displays how battery heat generation is distributed on the battery cells.

Running a Simcenter STAR-CCM+ Simulation with a Single Cell

If you have not already done so, download the tutorial files bundle. See Downloading the Tutorial Files from the Support Center Portal.

Preparing Files in Battery Design Studio®

Prepare battery data in BDS and import it into Simcenter STAR-CCM+.

Battery Design Studio (BDS) is a tool for the design, simulation, and analysis of batteries. Battery data from BDS is imported into Simcenter STAR-CCM+ and can be used to set up complex scenarios, such as simulating cooling by including a fluid region around the battery cells.

To use a battery cell in a Simcenter STAR-CCM+ simulation, the following files must be generated in BDS:

• .tbm—a text battery model file, containing all the information about the battery. This information includes construction, sizing, materials, and physics models.

• .prg—a program file, containing details of the battery load cycle

With Simcenter STAR-CCM+, it is possible to import battery data from BDS and set up complex scenarios that include a fluid region around the battery cells to simulate cooling.

In the following topics, tbm and prg files are generated for a lithium-ion battery cell in BDS.

If you do not wish to work through the steps involving BDS, you can jump directly to Running a Simcenter STAR-CCM+ simulation with a Single Cell.

Contents:

Creating a Battery Cell

Creating a Program File

Creating a Battery Cell

Create a battery cell in BDS.

Use the Li-Ion stack cell that is available in BDS as a starting point.

To create a battery cell in BDS:

1. Launch BDS.

2. Create a workspace by selecting File > New Workspace.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10913

The New Workspace dialog appears.

3. Enter BasicCell as the Name in the textbox, and select an appropriate location.

4. Click OK.

5. If the location does not exist, confirm the directory creation.

Components of the battery are created using the tree on the left of the BDS interface. Create a battery cell.

6. Right-click the Batteries folder and select Add New Battery > LiIon Stack > LiIonStack.

A new node, LiIonStack, is added below the Batteries node folder, and a corresponding .tbm file is created in the workspace directory.

The cell can be renamed immediately after it is created.

7. Rename the battery cell TutorialCell.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10914

8. To see a diagram of the battery cell, select Main in the TutorialCell.tbm feature tree.

The position of the tabs on each electrode is specified using an offset value. To reposition the tabs, change the offset values.

9. Select the + Electrode node in the TutorialCell.tbm window.

10.Set Tab offset (Otab) to 3.500.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10915

11.Select the - Electrode node in the TutorialCell.tbm window.

12.Set Tab offset (Otab) to 50.500.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10916

Select a battery model. This model defines how the battery behaves in response to different electrical loads. In this tutorial, the NTGPTable 3D model is used.

13.Scroll down to the Models node in the TutorialCell.tbm window, and select the NTGPTable 3D model from the IET folder.

The addition of a * to the TutorialCell.tbm window title indicates that you have changed the cell definition. Once the asterisk appears, Build the cell. This process rewrites the .tbm file in the workspace directory and prompts BDS to check the cell definition for any invalid changes.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10917

14.Right-click the Batteries > TutorialCell node in the BDS feature tree and select Build.

15.If prompted to save, accept.

A message box appears informing you that the build was successful.

16.Click OK to close the message box.

The cell definition is complete.

Creating a Program File

Create a program file in BDS.

The next step is to define a procedure for cycling the battery. In this case, specify a constant current discharge of 10 A, for 1 hour. The capacity of the cell is 10 Ah, so this procedure is equivalent to a 1 C discharge. You can find out the cell capacity by selecting the Report node in the TutorialCell.tbm window, and reading the value from the Cell Properties table.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10918

To create a procedure:

1. Right-click the Procedures node and select Add new procedure > IET Cycler.

The IET Cycler is a simulation model that allows you to define the Current (I), Voltage (E), and Temperature (T). A Cycler node is added under the Procedures folder, and a corresponding program file (.prg) is created in the workspace directory. A new window that is called Cycler.prg appears in the work area.

2. Rename the program file Tutorial1CDischarge.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10919

The name of the Cycler.prg window changes to Tutorial1CDischarge.prg.

3. Click <add> under the Type column for the Step in the Tutorial1CDischarge.prg window.

4. Click the cell twice for the drop-down menu to appear and select Discharge.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10920

The constant current discharge is specified as a Control Condition.

5. Click in the first cell of the Type column for the Control Condition and select Current.

6. Enter 10A as the Value.

The discharge finishes after 1 hour, which is specified as an End Condition.

7. Click in the Type column for the End Condition and select Time from the drop-down list.

8. Set the Value of Time to 3600s.

9. Click <add> under the Type column for the Step and select End.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10921

The definition of the battery cell and program is now complete.

10.Save the workspace by selecting File > Save Workspace from the menu.

11.Click Yes.

Running a Simcenter STAR-CCM+ Simulation with a Single Cell

Import the files from BDS into Simcenter STAR-CCM+ and run a simple single cell simulation.

Simcenter STAR-CCM+ 2020.3  |  User Guide

Siemens Digital Industries Software 10922

In this section of the tutorial, the files that you created in BDS are imported into Simcenter STAR-CCM+, and a simple single cell simulation is run.

To create the simulation:

If you skipped the section involving BDS, create a working directory and copy the files that are required for this tutorial.

1. Create a working directory called BasicCell.

2. Navigate to the battery folder of the downloaded tutorial files, and copy the following files into the BasicCell directory:

◦ TutorialCell.tbm

◦ Tutorial1CDischarge.prg

Create the simulation.

3. Launch Simcenter STAR-CCM+.

4. Start a simulation.

5. Save the simulation as batteryTutorial.sim in the BasicCell directory.
